focus: Duplicate provisioning, part 2: design and size the fix (actions/cache vs reusable workflow vs one provisioning job feeding artifacts), with risks

graphEvents.label: How should the duplicated provision_worktree work across the three workflows be removed

label: provision_worktree skips a package when _wn_deps_satisfied finds the first non-@spec-kit dependency name in some ancestor node_modules, comparing no version, lockfile hash or timestamp. That name-presence walk is what makes an actions/cache restore usable at all, and it is also why an incomplete cache key produces a green run against wrong dependency versions instead of a red one.

Build stamps live under the worktree git dir at provision-stamps/<pkg>, hold a fingerprint of the package's git-tracked inputs, and a missing stamp reports unrecorded and forces a rebuild. actions/checkout creates a fresh .git each run, so caching node_modules and dist alone still rebuilds all five artifacts; caching .git/provision-stamps with them skips the builds exactly when the tracked sources match, because a stamp from another commit mismatches and rebuilds.

The provisioned dependency set measures 2,323,104 KB (about 2.22 GB) uncompressed across the ten trees that hold node_modules, dominated by spec-kit at 634 MB, .skilled at 483 MB and the advisor runtime at 432 MB; the five build outputs total about 3.6 MB. The transfer is therefore the whole cache cost, and roughly 0.7-1 GB per compressed entry against a shared 10 GB per-repository cache budget.

Recommended fix: one composite action at .github/actions/provision-deps holding actions/cache/restore, a bun install gated on a cache miss, provision_worktree unconditionally as the authority, and actions/cache/save gated on a miss. The key globs **/package-lock.json, **/bun.lock, **/bun.lockb plus the path list and the provisioning script; there are no restore-keys, and .git/provision-stamps rides in the same entry as the artifacts.

Sized on the measured medians (provision 63/64/60 s per job, job medians 194/138/144 s): the hit path takes hooks 194 to about 154 s, plugin tests 138 to 98 and each dual-version leg 144 to 104, so billed minutes per commit fall 16 to 11 when all three fire, about 145 billed minutes per day (3.8 percent of 3812) and about 40 s of wall clock on each of the five jobs. This is steady state; every lockfile change costs one cold run.

The artifact feed is rejected on three grounds: artifacts do not cross workflows without workflow_run, which serializes consumers behind a completed producer run; it hands 2.2 GB to each of four consumers instead of one cache entry restored concurrently; and the merge it requires widens opencode-dual-version's narrow path set to the plugin-tests superset, producing more runs. A reusable workflow deduplicates definitions, not work, since each call site still gets its own runner and checkout, and the three job bodies differ by matrix, a second job, a git identity step and a leg-pinned bun suite.

Each of the three workflows names only its own file in its path filters, so after the shared action lands an edit to it re-runs none of the five consumers. Two guards close it: add .github/actions/** to all three path lists, and add a case to check-gate-inputs.sh, which already loops every workflow file, asserting that a workflow naming a local .github/actions path names it in both filters.

The cache's real risk is silence rather than staleness: the cache-miss path is the only thing that proves provision_worktree still works against today's lockfiles, so a warm cache lets a change that breaks a cold install ship green. Mitigation is a use-cache input defaulting to true plus one scheduled cold run per week.

Sequencing correction to iteration 003: the cache is a win on both axes (PR wait 194 to about 154 s, 16 to 11 billed minutes per commit), while the hook-into-plugin merge is a minutes-for-latency trade (14 to 10 billed minutes but 154 to 230 s of wait once cached). Shipping the merge first would be worse on both axes than shipping the cache first, so the cache must land first and the merge becomes optional.
Provisioning stays the authority: every consumer runs provision_worktree after any cache restore, so a restored tree the walk rejects is reinstalled rather than trusted.
No restore-keys on a cache that seeds a name-presence dependency walk: a partial-key restore hands the walk a tree whose versions nothing checks.
A cache entry that carries build output must carry the build stamps in the same entry, so a hit skips builds and a mismatched fingerprint still rebuilds.
Any workflow that uses a local .github/actions path must name that path in both its push and pull_request filters.

direction: One provisioning job uploading an artifact that the three workflows consume
reason: Artifacts do not cross workflow boundaries without workflow_run, which serializes consumers behind a completed producer run, ships 2.2 GB to each consumer, and requires merging the workflows first - which widens the dual-version path filter to the plugin-tests superset and causes more runs.

direction: Reusable workflow (workflow_call) as the dedupe mechanism
reason: A called workflow runs as the caller's job on its own runner after its own checkout, so it deduplicates definitions and never the provision work; absorbing whole jobs would require parameterizing a matrix, a second job, a git identity step and a leg-pinned suite into one body.

direction: actions/cache restore-keys for a partial match
reason: A fallback key restores a tree from a different lockfile set, which the name-presence dependency walk accepts silently; a cold run costs 62 s, while a wrong-version green run costs the purpose of the gate.

direction: setup-node cache: npm as the fix for the provisioned trees
reason: It caches the npm download cache only, so it shortens npm ci on a cold provision and does nothing on an already-satisfied tree; the minute cost is the install plus build, not the tarball fetch.
